title: Marbling two underglazes on bisqueware
subtitle: Swirled underglaze decoration applied to fired bisqueware, sealed with a clear glaze
excerpt: Marbling is achieved by swirling two contrasting underglazes together before they dry. Applied to bisqueware and sealed with a clear glaze, the swirled pattern fires to a smooth marbled surface. The technique requires bisque-fired ware and a glaze firing. This tutorial covers the underglaze marbling process.
sourceNotes: Underglaze marbling technique derived from traditional slip-and-glaze surface decoration practice. English slipware marbling documented from the seventeenth century onward; modern underglaze adaptation derived from studio practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: Pottery that has been through a first firing (around cone 06) to harden the clay body, making it porous and ready for glaze decoration.
A ceramic colourant applied before the glaze layer. Fires to a fixed colour under a clear glaze.
The second kiln firing, at the clay body's mature temperature, which melts the glaze to a glass-like surface.

content.text: This technique requires two kiln firings: a bisque firing at cone 06 (approximately 1000°C) and a glaze firing at the clay body's mature temperature. Studio or community kiln access is needed.
Marbling with underglazes is different from slip-marbling on green clay. On
bisque
-fired ware the
underglaze

is brushed onto the surface and the two colours are swirled before they dry. The bisque surface is porous enough to grip the underglaze but not so absorbent that the liquid disappears immediately: there is a working window of 30 to 60 seconds during which the colours can be moved.
What you need

Bisque-fired stoneware or earthenware pieces. Two contrasting ready-mixed underglazes (for example, white and cobalt blue, or cream and rust). A wide mop brush and a liner brush. A clear low-fire glaze (if the underglaze is rated for low fire) or clear mid-fire glaze for stoneware.
The marbling process
Clean the bisque surface with a dry cloth to remove any dust or kiln wash residue. Dust reduces underglaze adhesion.
Apply the first underglaze colour broadly across the surface with the mop brush. Work quickly and do not over-brush: the bisque absorbs the liquid fast and re-working creates drag marks.

Marbling with underglazes is different from slip-marbling on green clay. On bisque-fired ware, brush both colours onto the surface and swirl them before they dry. The bisque is porous enough to grip the underglaze. It is not so absorbent that the liquid disappears at once. You have 30 to 60 seconds to move the colours before they set.

Swirl the two colours together using a clean liner brush or a dry feather: drag the brush through both wet colours in long, curving strokes. Vary the pressure and direction: some strokes tight and curving, some long and fluid. Do not over-mix or the colours will merge into a single muddy tone. Four to six swirl strokes is usually enough.
Allow the underglaze to dry fully: 15 to 20 minutes. For multi-piece sessions, move to the next piece immediately while the swirl on the previous one dries.

Apply a clear glaze over the dried underglaze: either by dipping in a glaze bucket, pouring, or brushing two coats with the mop brush. The clear glaze must be rated for the same temperature as the clay body. Apply to a thickness of 1 mm (three brush coats or a 3-second dip).
Load into the kiln with stilts if needed (to protect the kiln shelf from glaze drips at the base). Fire to the
glaze firing
temperature appropriate for the clay body.
What it looks like when right

After firing, the clear glaze should be smooth and glassy with the marbled underglaze visible beneath as a crisp swirled pattern. The two colours should remain distinct: the swirl edges clean-cut rather than blurred. Where the colours overlap during application they may merge slightly, creating a third tone where the two meet.
Common mistakes
Over-swirling: the colours merge into a single brownish-grey tone. Stop after four to six strokes, before the distinct colours blend fully.
Underglaze lifts or flakes under the clear glaze: the bisque surface was dusty. Clean with a dry cloth before applying.

Pattern muddy and indistinct after firing: the clear glaze was applied too thick and flowed over the underglaze boundary during firing. Apply glaze at correct thickness and do not apply to an area the glaze will run off.

rows.problem: Underglaze dry before second colour applied
rows.cause: Bisque very porous; first colour applied too thinly
rows.fix: Pre-dampen the bisque lightly with a damp sponge before applying underglaze: this slows the absorption and extends the working time slightly.

rows.problem: Colours look dull and flat after firing
rows.cause: Clear glaze too thin; underglaze layer too thin
rows.fix: Apply underglaze in two coats, allowing each coat to dry between applications. Apply clear glaze to full 1 mm thickness.
